wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for mint jelly: an infusion of fresh mint made into a jelly with sugar, lemon juice and liquid pectin and processed in a boiling-water bath.

sekcje.naglowek: Why you must not change the recipe
akapity: The FDA list gives parsley, a garden herb, a pH of about 5.70–6.00; herbs and infusions made from them are not naturally acidic, so a herb jelly can be canned only with a tested amount of added acid and sugar, as in this recipe.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not change the amounts of the acid ingredient (lemon juice) or of the mint juice; the recipe is tested only in the proportions given.
NCHFP warns not to reduce the sugar in traditional recipes: too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.

For about 3 or 4 half-pint jars NCHFP uses 1 3/4 cups of mint juice (made from 1 1/2 cups of firmly packed fresh mint and 2 1/4 cups of water), 3 1/2 cups of sugar, 2 tablespoons of lemon juice and 1 pouch (3 ounces) of liquid pectin.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use bottled lemon juice in the amount given; NCHFP notes, in its lemon curd recipe, that fresh lemon juice can vary in acidity.
Sterilize the jars and prepare two-piece lids according to the manufacturer.
NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars.
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet.
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it.
Wash the mint and crush or finely chop the leaves and stems.
Put the mint in a saucepan, add the water and bring quickly to a boil.
Remove from the heat, cover and let stand for 10 minutes.
Strain out the mint and discard it.
Measure 1 3/4 cups of mint juice into a large saucepot and stir in the sugar and lemon juice.
Over high heat, stirring constantly, bring to a full boil that cannot be stirred down.
Add the liquid pectin, bring back to a full rolling boil and boil hard for 1 minute.
Remove from the heat and quickly skim off the foam.
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time.
Pour the hot jelly immediately into hot, sterile jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace.
Wipe the jar rims with a damp clean paper towel, put on two-piece metal lids and process in a boiling-water canner.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 5 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 10 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
Keep opened jelly in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or lower.
Discard jelly with mold on it; USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest.
